as_read: Conflicting: the one trial of coffeeberry extract alone at the label's 100 mg found no benefit and a small negative signal, while other extract trials report selected cognitive or skill gains, so there is no clear benefit.

quote.text: Overall, the findings of the current study suggest that coffeeberry extract at a low or moderate dose does not have a beneficial effect on mood, mental and physical energy levels, or cognition; higher doses, as have been administered previously, may be more effective.

proposed_decision_text: The one label, Neuro Shred, prints NeuroFactor 100 mg, dried whole coffee fruit concentrate, in a formula with three caffeine rows, Morosil, Capsimax and other actives. The on-target trial 37299382 gave 100 mg or 300 mg coffeeberry extract alone to 72 healthy adults in a double-blind crossover; 300 mg had no effect, and 100 mg increased mental fatigue and decreased accuracy on a sustained attention task, which the authors say to read with caution. It is acute and its abstract names no primary outcome. Other trials conflict. 33498314, a pilot crossover at 100 mg in older adults, reported decreased reaction time and increased BDNF. 39064791 at 200 mg reported better working memory accuracy against placebo. 31829793 reported shorter reaction time in 71 adults with mild cognitive decline with no main effect on accuracy and no amount in the abstract. 40993029 at 300 mg improved short passing only, and 34380382 at 1100 mg reported alerting effects with limited cognitive effects. The stored 23312069 is a single dose raising plasma BDNF 143% from baseline in 10 people, with no cognitive outcome. This is conflicting evidence with no clear benefit, and the labelled formula's caffeine rows can't be separated from the concentrate. Abstracts only.

studies_to_add.primary_endpoint: No primary outcome named in the abstract; cognition, mood and subjective energy at 60 and 120 minutes
studies_to_add.quote: Analysis revealed no effect of 300 mg coffeeberry extract, while 100 mg resulted in increased mental fatigue during the performance of cognitively demanding tasks (p = 0.025) and decreased accuracy on a task of sustained attention (p = 0.003), compared to placebo, at 60 min post dose.

stop_list: The label row's canonical id is neurofactor, not coffeeberry: name NeuroFactor, form dried whole coffee fruit concentrate, 100 mg, on label 78153. The21 lists the label under coffeeberry, and no active row carries that id. A separate neurofactor record exists in the stored literature and I did not read it.
Fields can't hold acute-only null next to 28-day positive results.
The 37299382 extract is standardized to 40% chlorogenic acid and given as a beverage; the label does not print a standardization.
clinician_items: 37299382: 100 mg coffeeberry increased mental fatigue and decreased sustained attention accuracy at 60 minutes; authors caution given the number of outcomes.
stored_rating_note: Stored positive_weak rests on one 10-person single-dose BDNF change from baseline, with no cognition measured. The same trial backs coffee_fruit, so three canonical ids (coffeeberry, coffee_fruit, neurofactor) describe near the same material, and that split may be worth a look. Its study_type is outside rct and systematic_review_meta.
